warmup.q: The house bell is MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = DROP_LATEST). A quick waiter and a diary keeper who needs 1 s per line both subscribe. Six announcements are emitted 10 ms apart. What does the quick waiter receive?
options: All six: DROP_LATEST only drops values for the slow subscriber
1, 2 and 3: announcements 4, 5 and 6 are dropped for everyone
1 and 2: the buffer holds two values
warmup.why: Every subscriber reads from one shared buffer. The diary keeper took 1 and is busy, so 2 and 3 fill the two slots it still needs. When 4 arrives the buffer is full, and DROP_LATEST throws 4 away before anyone can read it, the waiter included. The same happens to 5 and 6.

opening:
The busy house from the coroutines track has two ways to tell people things. In the hall hangs the menu board, which always shows the latest choice. In the kitchen hangs the house bell, which the cook rings for each announcement: soup's ready, the bread is here, clear the table. Tonight the bell has a small slate beside it, and the cook chalks each announcement on it, so that a listener who was busy can catch up. Two people listen: the waiter, who is quick, and the diary keeper, who copies every announcement into the kitchen diary by hand.

The diary keeper falls behind, and the waiter starts missing announcements, though he was never slow at all. The easy trap is to picture a slate for each listener.

In Errors, completion, retries and timeouts, every collector cooked its own recipe. Hot flows share. In this lesson, we'll find who decides when the slate is full, write the exact rule for emit and tryEmit, read the menu board closely, and share one cooking session among many diners. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a bell, a slate, a quick waiter and a slow diary keeper. A SharedFlow has one slate for every subscriber, so the slowest one sets the pace or the losses, and the default flow has no slate at all. A StateFlow is the menu board: one slot, compared with equals. shareIn and stateIn give a shared cooking session one cook, started and stopped by SharingStarted.

Now search your own code for stateIn( and check who reads the result. If nothing collects it, WhileSubscribed never starts.

Next, we'll connect flows to the world outside. How do you turn an old probe that calls you back into a flow, without losing readings or leaving its listener behind?

sections.h: One slow subscriber decides what the quick one gets
sections.html:
A cold flow is a recipe card: every collector, the code that calls collect to receive its values, cooks it again from the top. A hot flow runs whether or not anyone collects it, and shares each value with whoever is listening at that moment. A MutableSharedFlow is a hot flow that you send values into by hand with emit, and it is the house bell. Each collector of a hot flow is a subscriber.

A helper wired up the bell like this, with one coroutine (a light piece of work that can pause without holding a thread) per listener. The waiter is quick. The diary keeper needs a full second per line, so the helper picked DROP_LATEST: when the diary keeper falls behind, the bell should drop announcements while the waiter carries on.

Java
// Java equivalent: a Reactor multicast sink; the diary subscriber requests one item, then stalls
Sinks.Many<Integer> bell = Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing();
bell.asFlux().subscribe(waiter::add);          // quick: unbounded demand
bell.asFlux().subscribe(diaryThatRequestsOne); // slow: request(1), then nothing
for (int a = 1; a <= 6; a++) bell.tryEmitNext(a);
Kotlin
val bell = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST)
backgroundScope.launch { bell.collect { waiter += it } }                // quick
backgroundScope.launch { bell.collect { diary += it; delay(1_000) } }   // 1 s per line
for (announcement in 1..6) { bell.emit(announcement); delay(10) }

extraBufferCapacity = 2 gives the slate room for two announcements, and onBufferOverflow says what to do when it is full. Predict what the waiter receives. Here is the output in virtual time, the fake clock of runTest that skips over waits, with the other two choices for comparison:

DROP_LATEST   waiter got [1, 2, 3]            diary got [1, 2, 3]
SUSPEND       waiter got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]   diary got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]   emit(4), (5), (6) returned at t=1000, 2000, 3000
DROP_OLDEST   waiter got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]   diary got [1, 5, 6]

The waiter lost 4, 5 and 6, and he was never slow. To see why, look at the slate. There is one slate beside the bell, and every subscriber reads it at their own pace, keeping their place with a finger. A line can be wiped only when every listener has read it. So the slowest listener decides when the slate is full, for everyone. There is no slate per listener.

Walk through it. The diary keeper takes 1 and starts a line that takes a second. Announcements 2 and 3 go onto the slate, which has room for exactly two. The waiter reads them at once, but that wipes nothing, because the diary keeper still needs them. Announcement 4 finds the slate full, and the overflow policy, what a full buffer does with a new value, decides what happens:

  • SUSPEND, the default: emit(4) waits until the diary keeper takes 2, at t=1000. The waiter has nothing new to read, so he waits as well.
  • DROP_LATEST: 4 is never chalked up. Nobody hears it, the waiter included.
  • DROP_OLDEST: 4 is chalked over 2, and the diary keeper's finger is pushed past the wiped line. Only the slow listener skips.

That makes the overflow policy a choice about every subscriber at once. When no announcement may be lost and the waiter must not wait, keep SUSPEND and give the slow listener a shelf of its own. bell.buffer(64).collect { ... } puts a channel, a queue between coroutines, between the slate and the slow work (the shelf from Buffering), so the diary keeper copies each line off the slate at once. In the Try it, that version delivers all six to both, and every emit returns by t=50. The shelf has a size: once its 64 spots fill, the diary keeper stops taking from the slate, and everyone waits again.

A SharedFlow has one buffer for all its subscribers. Give a slow subscriber a buffer of its own.

The picture breaks at the cook's hand. A real cook would just ring louder and carry on. With SUSPEND, she stands with the chalk raised until the slowest listener has read a line. The exact rule behind all this is short enough to fit in two lines, and it also says when tryEmit answers no.

code.title: FastAndSlow.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest // One house bell with a slate, two listeners: the waiter, who is fast, and the diary keeper, who // copies each announcement into the kitchen diary by hand, 1,000 ms a line. Six announcements, 10 ms apart. // All times are virtual milliseconds (runTest), so the output is the same on every run. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun bellWith(policy: BufferOverflow, diaryHasOwnBuffer: Boolean = false) = runTest { val bell = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = policy) val waiter = mutableListOf<Int>() val diary = mutableListOf<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { bell.collect { waiter += it } } val diarySide = if (diaryHasOwnBuffer) bell.buffer(64) else bell // a channel of its own in front of the slow work backgroundScope.launch { diarySide.collect { diary += it; delay(1_000) } } runCurrent() // both have subscribed and wait for a value val returned = mutableListOf<String>() for (announcement in 1..6) { bell.emit(announcement) returned += "$announcement@t=$currentTime" delay(10) } advanceTimeBy(10_000); runCurrent() println(if (diaryHasOwnBuffer) "$policy, the diary collects bell.buffer(64)" else "$policy") println(" waiter got $waiter") println(" diary got $diary") println(" emit returned: $returned") } fun main() { bellWith(BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) bellWith(BufferOverflow.SUSPEND) bellWith(BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) bellWith(BufferOverflow.SUSPEND, diaryHasOwnBuffer = true) }

alt.html: package workbench.flows.l07; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import org.reactivestreams.Subscription; import reactor.core.publisher.BaseSubscriber; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; // Java equivalent: Reactor multicast sinks with one fast subscriber and one slow one. // The slow diary keeper asks for one announcement and then nothing more until the end, // as if stuck on its first line. Everything runs on the main thread, so no timing is involved. public class FastAndSlowJava { static final class SlowDiary extends BaseSubscriber<Integer> { final List<Integer> got = new ArrayList<>(); @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(1); } @Override protected void hookOnNext(Integer v) { got.add(v); } } static void run(String label, Sinks.Many<Integer> bell, boolean diaryHasOwnBuffer) { List<Integer> waiter = new ArrayList<>(); bell.asFlux().subscribe(waiter::add); // unbounded demand SlowDiary diary = new SlowDiary(); // demand of 1, or a buffer of its own in front of the slow work (diaryHasOwnBuffer ? bell.asFlux().onBackpressureBuffer(64) : bell.asFlux()).subscribe(diary); List<String> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (int a = 1; a <= 6; a++) results.add(a + "=" + bell.tryEmitNext(a)); String waiterBefore = waiter.toString(); diary.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); // the diary keeper catches up at the end System.out.println(label); System.out.println(" tryEmitNext: " + results); System.out.println(" waiter had " + waiterBefore + " while the diary keeper was stuck"); System.out.println(" waiter got " + waiter); System.out.println(" diary got " + diary.got); } public static void main(String[] args) { run("multicast().directAllOrNothing()", Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing(), false); run("multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(1, false)", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(1, false), false); // one slot run("multicast().directBestEffort()", Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort(), false); run("onBackpressureBuffer(1, false), the diary subscribes through onBackpressureBuffer(64)", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(1, false), true); } }

try.expect: DROP_LATEST: both get [1, 2, 3], and every emit returns at once. SUSPEND: both get all six, but emit(4), emit(5) and emit(6) return at t=1000, 2000 and 3000, so the quick waiter waits for the diary keeper. DROP_OLDEST: the waiter gets all six and the diary keeper [1, 5, 6]. With bell.buffer(64) on the diary side, both get all six and every emit returns by t=50. With a buffer of 3, DROP_LATEST gives both [1, 2, 3, 4], and under SUSPEND the first to wait is emit(5), which returns at t=1000. The Java twin shows the same choices with Reactor sinks: directAllOrNothing() refuses 2 to 6 for both subscribers (FAIL_OVERFLOW), a one-slot onBackpressureBuffer holds the waiter at [1] while the diary keeper is stuck, directBestEffort() drops only for the stalled subscriber (a setting Kotlin's SharedFlow doesn't have), and onBackpressureBuffer(64) on the diary side frees the waiter.

sections.h: The exact rule: count what the slowest subscriber hasn't taken
sections.html:
emit is two steps in the source: if (tryEmit(value)) return, and only then suspend. tryEmit is the version that never waits: it returns true if it handled the value, and false if it would have had to wait. So one rule answers both questions, when emit waits and when tryEmit says no.

  1. With no subscribers, every call succeeds. The value goes into the replay cache if replay > 0, the last few values kept for subscribers who arrive later, and nowhere otherwise. extraBufferCapacity plays no part: with replay = 2, extraBufferCapacity = 10, five emits to nobody leave replayCache = [4, 5].
  2. With subscribers, the slate holds replay + extraBufferCapacity values, and it is full when the slowest subscriber has that many values it has not taken yet. Then SUSPEND makes tryEmit return false and emit wait, while the two drop policies return true and drop.

"Taken" has an exact meaning. A subscriber takes a value when it reads it off the slate, before your collect lambda runs. A value that a busy subscriber is still working on no longer counts. That is why the diary keeper held only 2 and 3 against the slate in the first section, and not 1.

Now the default, MutableSharedFlow(), with no replay and no extra buffer. There is no slate at all, so a value can only pass hand to hand. That is a rendezvous, the hand-over from Buffering where both hands must meet: emit holds the note out until every listener has a hand on it. tryEmit can't wait, so it lets go of the note, and the note falls. It therefore returns false whenever there is a subscriber, even an idle one, as lesson 8 of the coroutines track said. And emit returns the moment the subscriber takes the value, before the subscriber has done anything with it: with 100 ms of work per value, emit(1), emit(2) and emit(3) return at t=0, 100 and 200.

Here is the rule at work. One subscriber has subscribed and waits, and then tryEmit(1) to tryEmit(6) run back to back (T is true, f is false):

Flow tryEmit(1..6) The subscriber gets
MutableSharedFlow(), no subscriber T T T T T T (nobody there)
MutableSharedFlow() f f f f f f nothing
extraBufferCapacity = 2 T T f f f f 1, 2
replay = 2 T T f f f f 1, 2
replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 2 T T T f f f 1, 2, 3
extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST T T T T T T 5, 6
extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_LATEST T T T T T T 1, 2

Two rows deserve a second look. While someone is subscribed, replay = 2 behaves exactly like extraBufferCapacity = 2: both are lines on the one slate. And three idle subscribers give the same row as one, because they share the slate.

The slate also explains a subscriber who arrives late. Someone who walks into the kitchen late reads the lines kept for latecomers, the replay cache, and then hears new announcements. They never see the lines that the slow diary keeper is still working through. With replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 10, a subscriber stuck on value 1 while 1 to 5 are emitted works through all five, and a second subscriber who joins after 5 gets only [5].

Count what the slowest subscriber hasn't taken. That number decides every emit.

Check yourself: with extraBufferCapacity = 3, SUSPEND and one waiting subscriber, which call is the first tryEmit to return false? The bell keeps every line until the slowest reader is done. The menu board keeps one.

code.html: package workbench.flows.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest // When does tryEmit return false? One subscriber subscribes and waits, then tryEmit(1..6) // runs back to back, so the subscriber can't take anything between two calls. Virtual time. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun table(label: String, flow: MutableSharedFlow<Int>, subscribers: Int = 1) = runTest { val got = mutableListOf<Int>() repeat(subscribers) { s -> backgroundScope.launch { flow.collect { if (s == 0) got += it; delay(100) } } } runCurrent() val results = (1..6).map { flow.tryEmit(it) }.joinToString(" ") { if (it) "T" else "f" } advanceTimeBy(10_000); runCurrent() // advanceUntilIdle() would not run backgroundScope println("%-30s subscribers=%d tryEmit: %s received: %s".format(label, subscribers, results, got)) } // The rendezvous: with no buffer, emit waits until the subscriber has TAKEN the value. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun rendezvous() = runTest { val bus = MutableSharedFlow<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { println(" t=$currentTime subscriber took $it"); delay(100) } } runCurrent() for (v in 1..3) { bus.emit(v); println(" t=$currentTime emit($v) returned") } } // A late subscriber gets the replay cache, then live values. Never the slow one's backlog. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun late() = runTest { val bus = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 10) val s1 = mutableListOf<Int>(); val s2 = mutableListOf<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { s1 += it; delay(100) } } runCurrent() (1..5).forEach { bus.emit(it) } // S1 is still busy with 1 backgroundScope.launch { bus.collect { s2 += it } } advanceTimeBy(1_000); runCurrent() println(" S1 (there from the start) got $s1, S2 (joined after 5) got $s2") } fun main() { println("== tryEmit(1..6) with a waiting subscriber") table("MutableSharedFlow()", MutableSharedFlow(), subscribers = 0) table("MutableSharedFlow()", MutableSharedFlow()) table("MutableSharedFlow()", MutableSharedFlow(), subscribers = 3) table("extraBufferCapacity=2", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2)) table("replay=2", MutableSharedFlow(replay = 2)) table("replay=1, extra=2", MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 2)) table("extra=2, DROP_OLDEST", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)) table("extra=2, DROP_LATEST", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST)) println("== emit on MutableSharedFlow(), subscriber needs 100 ms per value") rendezvous() println("== a late subscriber, replay=1, extra=10") late() }

A subscriber says "I can take n" // with request(n) BEFORE anything is emitted, so a sink can push straight into it. public class OneTapeJava { static final class Waiting extends BaseSubscriber<Integer> { final List<Integer> got = new ArrayList<>(); @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(1); } // idle, ready for one @Override protected void hookOnNext(Integer v) { got.add(v); } } static void table(String label, Sinks.Many<Integer> sink, int subscribers) { Waiting first = null; for (int i = 0; i < subscribers; i++) { Waiting w = new Waiting(); sink.asFlux().subscribe(w); if (first == null) first = w; } List<String> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (int v = 1; v <= 6; v++) results.add(sink.tryEmitNext(v).toString()); if (first != null) first.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); System.out.printf("%-36s subscribers=%d %s received: %s%n", label, subscribers, results, first == null ? "[]" : first.got); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("== tryEmitNext(1..6), each subscriber has requested 1"); table("multicast().directAllOrNothing()", Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing(), 0); table("multicast().directAllOrNothing()", Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing(), 1); table("multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(2)", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(2, false), 1); table("replay().limit(2)", Sinks.many().replay().limit(2), 1); System.out.println("== a late subscriber to replay().limit(1)"); Sinks.Many<Integer> bus = Sinks.many().replay().limit(1); Waiting s1 = new Waiting(); bus.asFlux().subscribe(s1); for (int v = 1; v <= 5; v++) bus.tryEmitNext(v); // S1 is still on its first item List<Integer> s2 = new ArrayList<>(); bus.asFlux().subscribe(s2::add); s1.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); System.out.println(" S1 got " + s1.got + ", S2 (joined after 5) got " + s2); } }

try.expect: The lines match the table, and three subscribers give the same line as one. Each emit returns at the same virtual time as subscriber took, so it waits for the take, not for the 100 ms of work. The late subscriber gets [5] while the first one works through [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. In the Java twin the first tryEmitNext to an idle subscriber returns OK and the rest FAIL_OVERFLOW: a Reactor subscriber announces its demand with request(1) before anything is emitted, so the sink can hand one item straight over. With no subscriber Reactor answers FAIL_ZERO_SUBSCRIBER, where Kotlin answers true and the value goes nowhere. A replay().limit(2) sink accepts all six, and the stalled subscriber still gets all six once it asks: the limit only decides what a late subscriber gets, and the late subscriber to limit(1) gets [5], as in Kotlin.

sections.h: StateFlow is the menu board in the hall: one slot, compared with equals
sections.html:
A StateFlow is a hot flow that always holds exactly one current value, .value. Setting it replaces the old value, and collectors get the new one. It is the menu board in the hall: one slot. Two rules follow, and both compare with equals, the type's own idea of "the same".

Pinning up an equal card does nothing. The setter checks the new value against the current one and returns early when they are equal: no collector wakes up, and the old object stays on the board. After board.value = MenuItem("soup of the day", BigDecimal("4.50")) on a board that holds an equal item, board.value === first is still true. Equality is whatever your type says, so BigDecimal("4.500") counts as a new price, because BigDecimal.equals compares the number of decimal places too.

Each reader remembers the last card they read. A collector that wakes up reads the slot, and it emits only if the value differs from the one it emitted last. A busy collector skips everything in between, even a value that went away and came back:

Java
// Java equivalent: Reactor skips repeats and in-between values only when you add both operators
Sinks.Many<String> soup = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault("tomato");
soup.asFlux().onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged().subscribe(busyReader);
soup.tryEmitNext("leek");
soup.tryEmitNext("tomato");
// busyReader got [tomato]; without the two operators it gets all three
Kotlin
val soup = MutableStateFlow("tomato")
launch { soup.collect { log += it; delay(100) } }   // 100 ms of work per value
delay(10); soup.value = "leek"
delay(10); soup.value = "tomato"
// log is [tomato]: the board changed twice, and the busy reader saw nothing new

The busy reader looked up, saw tomato, and concluded that nothing had happened. As far as the board knows, nothing had. A diary built on a StateFlow loses exactly these changes. Use a StateFlow for state, and a SharedFlow for events.

Writes go through compare-and-set, an update that succeeds only if nobody changed the value since you read it. update { it + 1 } is a loop: read the value, compute the next one, call compareAndSet(prev, next), and go round again if another writer got in first. With 8 coroutines on Dispatchers.Default, which runs them on real threads, one per core, each adding 1 a hundred thousand times, the value ends at exactly 800,000, and the lambda ran more than that: 807,072 times in one run here, 1,405,098 in another. Any side effect inside update { }, such as a log line or a call, can run more than once. Compute inside the lambda and act after it.

compareAndSet compares with equals as well, which gives one odd case: compareAndSet(11, 11) on a board that holds 11 returns true, changes nothing and wakes nobody. Java's AtomicReference.compareAndSet compares references instead, so a fresh BigDecimal("10") fails against the stored one.

One counter does not skip anything: subscriptionCount, the number of current subscribers, as a StateFlow of its own. It works like a tally sheet by the hall door that marks every person coming and going. A subscriber that walks in and straight out still leaves +1 and -1 on the sheet. An observer saw [0, 1, 0] for such a visitor, where a plain StateFlow set to 1 and back to 0 showed only [0]. Sharing is built on this count.

A StateFlow keeps state, not history. When every change counts, use a SharedFlow.

Check yourself: a busy collector last saw tomato, and the soup goes leek, then pea. What does it see when it's free? Both kinds of hot flow so far were filled by hand. Most hot flows in real programs are a cold flow, shared.

code.html: package workbench.flows.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.update import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.test.UnconfinedTestDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import java.math.BigDecimal import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger data class MenuItem(val name: String, val price: BigDecimal) // A StateFlow is the menu board in the hall: one slot. Parts A, B, C and E use virtual time. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { runTest { println("== A: equal values") val first = MenuItem("soup of the day", BigDecimal("4.50")) val board = MutableStateFlow(first) val seen = mutableListOf<MenuItem>() backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { board.collect { seen += it } } board.value = MenuItem("soup of the day", BigDecimal("4.50")) // equal fields println(" after an equal set: board still holds the first object? ${board.value === first}") board.value = MenuItem("soup of the day", BigDecimal("4.500")) // one more zero println(" collector saw ${seen.map { it.price }}") } runTest { println("== B: tomato -> leek -> tomato while the collector is busy") val soup = MutableStateFlow("tomato") val log = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch { soup.collect { log += "t=$currentTime $it"; delay(100) } } runCurrent() delay(10); soup.value = "leek" delay(10); soup.value = "tomato" advanceTimeBy(500); runCurrent() println(" busy collector saw $log") } println("== C: compareAndSet") val count = MutableStateFlow(10) println(" cas(10, 11) = ${count.compareAndSet(10, 11)}, value ${count.value}") println(" cas(10, 12) = ${count.compareAndSet(10, 12)}, value ${count.value} (stale expect)") println(" cas(11, 11) = ${count.compareAndSet(11, 11)}, value ${count.value} (true, and nobody is woken)") println("== D: update { } from 8 coroutines x 100,000 on Dispatchers.Default (REAL threads)") val calls = AtomicInteger() val counter = MutableStateFlow(0) runBlocking(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(8) { launch { repeat(100_000) { counter.update { calls.incrementAndGet(); it + 1 } } } } } println(" value=${counter.value}, the lambda ran ${calls.get()} times") runTest { println("== E: subscriptionCount keeps every change") val events = MutableSharedFlow<Int>() val counts = mutableListOf<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { events.subscriptionCount.collect { counts += it } } runCurrent() val visitor = backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { events.collect { } } visitor.cancel() // joined and left before the observer ran again runCurrent() val plain = MutableStateFlow(0); val plainSeen = mutableListOf<Int>() backgroundScope.launch { plain.collect { plainSeen += it } } runCurrent() plain.value = 1; plain.value = 0; runCurrent() println(" subscriptionCount observer saw $counts; a plain StateFlow doing 0 -> 1 -> 0 showed $plainSeen") } }

alt.html: package workbench.flows.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import org.reactivestreams.Subscription; import reactor.core.publisher.BaseSubscriber; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; // Java equivalent: an AtomicReference for the value and a Reactor sink for the stream. // Reactor only conflates and de-duplicates if you ask for it with operators. public class NoticeBoardJava { record MenuItem(String name, BigDecimal price) {} static final class Busy extends BaseSubscriber<String> { final List<String> got = new ArrayList<>(); @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(1); } @Override protected void hookOnNext(String v) { got.add(v); } // then busy: asks for nothing more } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("== A: equal values"); System.out.println(" records with equal fields are equal: " + new MenuItem("soup of the day", new BigDecimal("4.50")).equals(new MenuItem("soup of the day", new BigDecimal("4.50")))); System.out.println(" 4.50 equals 4.500? " + new BigDecimal("4.50").equals(new BigDecimal("4.500")) + "; compareTo == 0? " + (new BigDecimal("4.50").compareTo(new BigDecimal("4.500")) == 0)); System.out.println("== B: tomato -> leek -> tomato while the subscriber is busy"); for (boolean asStateFlow : new boolean[] {false, true}) { Sinks.Many<String> soup = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault("tomato"); Busy busy = new Busy(); (asStateFlow ? soup.asFlux().onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged() : soup.asFlux()).subscribe(busy); soup.tryEmitNext("leek"); soup.tryEmitNext("tomato"); busy.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); // no longer busy System.out.println(" " + (asStateFlow ? "with onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged(): " : "plain replay sink: ") + busy.got); } System.out.println("== C: compareAndSet on AtomicReference compares references, not equals"); AtomicReference<BigDecimal> price = new AtomicReference<>(new BigDecimal("10")); System.out.println(" cas(new 10, 11) = " + price.compareAndSet(new BigDecimal("10"), new BigDecimal("11")) + ", value " + price.get()); System.out.println("== D: updateAndGet from 8 threads x 100,000 (REAL threads)"); AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicReference<Integer> counter = new AtomicReference<>(0); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) { threads.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) counter.updateAndGet(x -> { calls.incrementAndGet(); return x + 1; }); })); } for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.println(" value=" + counter.get() + ", the lambda ran " + calls.get() + " times"); System.out.println("== E: currentSubscriberCount() is a number you read, with no history"); Sinks.Many<Integer> events = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort(); System.out.println(" before: " + events.currentSubscriberCount()); events.asFlux().subscribe().dispose(); // a visitor joins and leaves System.out.println(" after a visitor came and went: " + events.currentSubscriberCount()); } }

try.expect: A: the board still holds the first object after the equal set, and the collector sees [4.50, 4.500]. B: only [t=0 tomato]. C: true, false, true, with the value still 11. D: exactly 800000, with the lambda run more than 800,000 times (807,072 in one run here). E: [0, 1, 0] against [0]. In the Java twin, BigDecimal.equals says 4.50 and 4.500 differ while compareTo says they are equal. The plain replay sink delivers all three soups, and the one with onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged() delivers only [tomato]. AtomicReference.compareAndSet fails because it compares references, and the expected BigDecimal is a different object. updateAndGet runs its lambda again on a conflict in the same way. currentSubscriberCount() is a plain number, 0 before and after the visitor, with no record of the visit.

sections.h: One cook for many diners: shareIn, stateIn and when the cook starts and stops
sections.html:
stateIn and shareIn read like conversions, but each one launches a coroutine. shareIn(scope, started, replay) creates a MutableSharedFlow with that replay, an extra buffer that brings it up to at least 64 slots, and SUSPEND. Then it launches one coroutine in scope, the owner that cancels all its coroutines when it is cancelled, and that coroutine collects the upstream, the cold flow above it, into the shared flow. stateIn does the same with a MutableStateFlow(initialValue).

Picture one cook and many diners. The sharing coroutine is the cook: she cooks the recipe once and serves every diner at the table. started, a SharingStarted value, decides when she works. Eagerly starts her at opening time, diners or not. Lazily lets the first diner get her started, and she never stops. WhileSubscribed(5_000) keeps her cooking while anyone is at the table and stops her 5 s after the last diner leaves, in case someone just stepped out.

Inside, WhileSubscribed watches subscriptionCount. When the count drops to 0, it waits for the stop timeout and then sends STOP, which cancels the upstream collection. A subscriber who comes back first cancels that pending wait, so the cook never stopped. The figure shows an exact virtual-time run for the oven thermometer, which sends run * 100 + i every second (made-up readings that show which run sent them). Screen A switches off at 2.5 s and is back at 4 s: it gets 104, from the same run. A goes off again at 6 s, and STOP comes at 11 s. When A comes back at 14 s, it gets the stale 111 first, and then 200 from run #2.

Three facts in that run catch people out:

  • The upstream restarts from the top, because it is a cold flow collected again. Run #2 counts from 200, and a running total built with runningFold would start over.
  • The returning subscriber sees the stale value first. replayExpirationMillis = 0 resets the StateFlow to its initial value when the cook stops, so the returning A gets -1 instead of 111.
  • With WhileSubscribed(), whose stop timeout is 0, every flicker of a screen is a STOP and a new START.
Java
// Java equivalent: connect with the first subscriber, disconnect 5 s after the last.
// After a disconnect Reactor reconnects with an empty replay cache, so no stale reading is shown.
Flux<Reading> live = thermometer.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5));
Kotlin
val live: StateFlow<Reading?> = thermometer.stateIn(
    houseScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0), initialValue = null)

Reading .value is not a subscription. It is glancing at the hall board from the doorway, and it doesn't call the cook. A hall board built with Lazily or WhileSubscribed and read only through .value never starts: in the Try it, three glances at 3.5 s read [null, null, null], and the thermometer was read 0 times. With Eagerly they read [180, 180, 180] after 4 readings.

Pick started by who reads. Code that only reads .value needs Eagerly.

Two more ways the sharing goes wrong. If the upstream throws, the sharing coroutine dies, and the exception goes to the scope's handler. The subscribers are not told. They sit at the table and wait for ever, so put retry or retryWhen above shareIn, as in the last lesson. And shareIn inside a function that each request calls starts a new cook per call: 50 calls that each read one value left 50 sharing coroutines and 500 upstream reads after 10 s. Fifty cooks, each one cooking for a diner who left after the first bite. Build the shared flow once, in a field, in a scope that you cancel when the program stops.

Check yourself: a screen goes off at 10 s and comes back at 13 s under WhileSubscribed(5_000). Does the thermometer restart? Everything here happens inside one Kotlin program, where every value arrives through emit. The outside world calls you back instead.

try.title: Watch the cook start, stop and start again
steps: Read SharingTimeline.kt. Before running it, write down when upstream START and STOP print, and what A gets each time it comes back.
Run it. Then run it with -Pargs=expire and with -Pargs=stop0, predicting each first.
Run the Java twin, the same script ten times faster on Reactor's replay(1).refCount. Compare the lines after A's second return.

code.title: SharingTimeline.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.SharingStarted import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.StateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.stateIn import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.StandardTestDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestCoroutineScheduler import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest // The oven thermometer, shared with stateIn. Each run of the upstream is numbered and emits // run * 100 + i every 1,000 ms (made-up readings), so you can see when a run starts over. Virtual time. private class Thermometer(private val clock: TestCoroutineScheduler) { var starts = 0 @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) val flow: Flow<Int> = flow { val run = ++starts println(" t=${clock.currentTime}: upstream START #$run") try { var i = 0 while (true) { emit(run * 100 + i++); delay(1_000) } } finally { println(" t=${clock.currentTime}: upstream STOP #$run") } } } @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun screen(started: SharingStarted) = runTest { println("== $started, initialValue = -1") val thermometer = Thermometer(testScheduler) val reading: StateFlow<Int> = thermometer.flow.stateIn(backgroundScope, started, initialValue = -1) fun open() = backgroundScope.launch { reading.collect { println(" t=$currentTime: A got $it") } } var a = open() delay(2_500); a.cancel(); println(" t=$currentTime: A leaves") delay(1_500); println(" t=$currentTime: A comes back"); a = open() delay(2_000); a.cancel(); println(" t=$currentTime: A leaves") delay(8_000); println(" t=$currentTime: A comes back"); open() delay(1_500); println(" t=$currentTime: end, upstream starts=${thermometer.starts}") } // A board that people only glance at with .value. Nobody collects it. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun readOnly() = runTest { println("== a hall board that people only read with .value") for (started in listOf(SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), SharingStarted.Lazily, SharingStarted.Eagerly)) { var fetches = 0 val feed = flow { while (true) { fetches++; emit(176 + fetches); delay(1_000) } } val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) val board: StateFlow<Int?> = feed.stateIn(scope, started, initialValue = null) delay(3_500) println(" $started: three glances read ${List(3) { board.value }}, upstream fetches=$fetches") scope.cancel() } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { when (args.firstOrNull()) { "expire" -> screen(SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0)) "stop0" -> screen(SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed()) else -> { screen(SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000)); readOnly() } } }

alt.title: SharingTimelineJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.flows.l07; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; // Java equivalent: Reactor's replay(1).refCount(1, grace), on the REAL clock. // Reactor's virtual clock lives in reactor-test, so this run is the Kotlin timeline // scaled down ten times: a reading every 100 ms and a 500 ms grace period. // Times vary by a few ms between runs. public class SharingTimelineJava { static long t0; static void log(String what) { if (t0 == 0) t0 = System.nanoTime(); // the clock starts at the first upstream START System.out.printf(" t=%4d ms: %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what); } static Disposable open(Flux<Integer> reading) { return reading.subscribe(v -> log("A got " + v)); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger starts = new AtomicInteger(); Flux<Integer> thermometer = Flux.defer(() -> { int run = starts.incrementAndGet(); log("upstream START #" + run); return Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofMillis(100)) .map(i -> run * 100 + i.intValue()) .doOnCancel(() -> log("upstream STOP #" + run)); }); Flux<Integer> reading = thermometer.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofMillis(500)); Disposable a = open(reading); Thread.sleep(250); a.dispose(); log("A leaves"); Thread.sleep(150); log("A comes back"); a = open(reading); Thread.sleep(200); a.dispose(); log("A leaves"); Thread.sleep(800); log("A comes back"); a = open(reading); Thread.sleep(150); a.dispose(); log("end, upstream starts=" + starts.get()); } }

try.expect: The default run: START #1 at 0, A gets 104 at 4000 with no restart, STOP #1 at 11000, and at 14000 A gets 111, then START #2 and 200, for 2 starts in all. In the .value part, WhileSubscribed and Lazily read [null, null, null] with 0 readings taken, and Eagerly reads [180, 180, 180] after 4. With expire, A gets -1 instead of 111 at 14000. With stop0, STOP #1 comes at 2500 and START #2 at 4000, where A gets the stale 102 and then 200; STOP #2 at 6000 and START #3 at 14000 make three starts. The Java twin keeps run #1 through the first return (A gets 104), stops about 500 ms after A leaves the second time, and on the late return prints START #2 and then 200 with no stale value, because Reactor's replay(1) begins a fresh cache for the new connection. Its times vary by a few ms.

compare.title: One oven thermometer, shared for the hall board and for the kitchen screens

java.title: OvenBoard.java (Reactor)
java.html: final class OvenBoard implements AutoCloseable { private final AtomicReference<Reading> latest = new AtomicReference<>(); private final Disposable boardConnection; final Flux<Reading> live; OvenBoard(Flux<Reading> thermometer) { // for the hall board: connect now, retry after a second, keep the latest in a field this.boardConnection = thermometer .retryWhen(Retry.fixedDelay(Long.MAX_VALUE, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException)) .subscribe(latest::set); // for the screens: connect with the first, disconnect 5 s after the last this.live = thermometer.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); } Reading current() { return latest.get(); } @Override public void close() { boardConnection.dispose(); } }

kotlin.title: OvenBoard.kt (StateFlow)
kotlin.html: class OvenBoard(thermometer: Flow<Reading>, scope: CoroutineScope) { // for the hall board: .value is not a subscription, so start now val board: StateFlow<Reading?> = thermometer .retry { e -> (e is IOException).also { if (it) delay(1_000) } } .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null) // for the screens: survive a 5 s flicker, then stop and forget the old reading val live: StateFlow<Reading?> = thermometer .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0), null) fun current(): Reading? = board.value } // cancelling `scope` stops both

compare.note: The Kotlin side needs no AtomicReference, because a StateFlow is both the holder and the stream: .value reads it at once, and collectors get the same value with equality checks built in. Lifetime differs too. Both Kotlin flows live in scope, so cancelling that one scope stops both upstream collections; in Reactor the board lives as long as its Disposable, and the screen connection as long as it has subscribers. The two sides also forget differently. After a disconnect, replay(1).refCount reconnects with an empty cache, and Kotlin needs replayExpirationMillis = 0 for the same effect. Errors are where they differ most. In Reactor an error in the thermometer reaches every subscriber as onError. In Kotlin it ends the sharing coroutine, goes to the scope, and leaves the subscribers waiting, which is why the retry sits above stateIn. Both versions open two connections to the thermometer, one per view.

worked.title: Share one order rail between the grill and the dessert station

steps.say: Orders arrive on a rail and are read off it one by one. Two stations need every order, the grill and the dessert station. Reading the rail twice would take every ticket twice, so the reading is shared with shareIn and replay = 0. The grill starts work at 250 ms and the dessert station at 500 ms. Predict what each has received by 800 ms.
steps.code: var next = 0 val orders = flow { while (true) { delay(100); emit("order-${next++}") } } // stands in for reading the rail val shared = orders.shareIn(houseScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly) // replay = 0 // the grill subscribes at t=250, desserts at t=500

alt.html: // Java equivalent: one connection, multicast to whoever is subscribed when an order arrives Flux<String> orders = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)).map(i -> "order-" + i); Flux<String> shared = orders.publish().autoConnect(0); // connect now, like Eagerly // the grill subscribes at t=250, desserts at t=500

steps.say: The virtual-time run. With Eagerly, order-0 and order-1 were read before anyone listened, and the dessert station also missed everything up to order-4. WhileSubscribed() helps the first station and not the second. With replay = 0, the slate keeps nothing for a late subscriber.
steps.code:
Eagerly:            grill=[order-2, order-3, order-4, order-5, order-6]  desserts=[order-5, order-6]
WhileSubscribed():  grill=[order-0, order-1, order-2, order-3, order-4]  desserts=[order-2, order-3, order-4]

steps.say: Start reading only when both stations are there. SharingStarted is a fun interface that turns the subscriber count into START and STOP commands, so the gate is one line. In the same run, both stations now get [order-0, order-1] by 800 ms.
steps.code: // 1. a strategy built on subscriptionCount val bothStations = SharingStarted { count -> count.map { if (it >= 2) SharingCommand.START else SharingCommand.STOP } } // 2. the same shareIn, gated val shared = orders.shareIn(houseScope, bothStations)

alt.html: // 1. and 2.: connect once two subscribers are there (Reactor's version never disconnects) Flux<String> shared = orders.publish().autoConnect(2);

steps.say: Self-check: the dessert station needs 50 ms per order and the grill needs 5 ms. With shareIn's default SUSPEND, which one sets the pace of reading the rail, and is that what you want here? (The dessert station. The slate is full once the slowest station has 64 orders it hasn't taken, and then emit, the reading, waits. For orders that must all be cooked, that is exactly the waiting you want. A drop policy would lose orders with no error.)

lab.title: Predict the slate, then share the oven thermometer two ways
steps: Run the tests. 24 of 25 fail: every SharedFlowRuleTest case and five of the six OvenBoardTest cases.

In SharedFlowRule.kt, write predictTryEmits from the rule in the second section, without creating a flow. For each row, the test runs a real MutableSharedFlow and compares. Then write predictReceived.
In OvenBoard.kt, fix hallBoard. People only read .value, so pick the SharingStarted that doesn't wait for a subscriber, and add a retry above stateIn that waits 1,000 ms after an IOException.
Fix screenFeed: survive a flicker within 5 s, stop 5 s after the last screen goes off, and reset to null when it stops.
Run the tests until all 25 pass. Then read how OvenBoardTest counts feed starts and stops in virtual time, and why it never calls advanceUntilIdle().
hints: The rule has three cases: no subscribers, a drop policy, and SUSPEND. In the last one the answer depends only on the number of the call and replay + extraBufferCapacity.
predictReceived: SUSPEND and DROP_LATEST keep the first values that fit, and DROP_OLDEST keeps the last ones.
retry { e -> ... } takes a suspending predicate, so it can delay(1_000) before it returns true. It must sit before stateIn: once the sharing coroutine has died, nothing restarts it.
If the late-screen test sees the old reading first, you need the second parameter of WhileSubscribed.

drill.title: A kitchen bell, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write class KitchenBell with fun ring(a: Announcement): Boolean, called from a callback that can't suspend (an old timer's callback, say), and val announcements: SharedFlow<Announcement>. A burst of up to 64 announcements must not be refused, no announcement may be dropped by a policy, and a slow diary keeper must not hold back a quick waiter. Write the diary keeper's collection too, and say in a comment when ring returns false.

answer.html: class KitchenBell { private val bell = MutableSharedFlow<Announcement>(extraBufferCapacity = 64) // SUSPEND, the default val announcements: SharedFlow<Announcement> = bell.asSharedFlow() // false only when some subscriber already has 64 announcements it hasn't taken; // the caller must not treat the announcement as delivered then. With no subscriber // it is always true, and the announcement goes nowhere. fun ring(a: Announcement): Boolean = bell.tryEmit(a) } // the diary keeper copies values off the shared buffer at once, into a channel of its own suspend fun keepDiary(bell: KitchenBell, diary: Diary) = bell.announcements.buffer(1_000).collect { diary.write(it) }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: a buffered multicast sink, and a buffer of its own on the diary side class KitchenBell { private final Sinks.Many<Announcement> bell = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); Flux<Announcement> announcements() { return bell.asFlux(); } // false when the buffer is full (FAIL_OVERFLOW); synchronized because a Reactor sink // refuses concurrent emits with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED synchronized boolean ring(Announcement a) { return bell.tryEmitNext(a).isSuccess(); } } Disposable keepDiary(KitchenBell bell, Diary diary) { return bell.announcements() .onBackpressureBuffer(1_000) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) .subscribe(diary::write); }

recap: A MutableSharedFlow is one buffer of replay + extraBufferCapacity slots shared by every subscriber. It is full when the slowest subscriber has that many values it hasn't taken, and a subscriber takes a value before its collect lambda runs.

When it is full, SUSPEND makes emit wait and tryEmit return false, DROP_LATEST drops the new value for everyone, and DROP_OLDEST makes only the slow subscriber skip. With no subscribers nothing ever waits. The default MutableSharedFlow() is a rendezvous: tryEmit fails whenever anyone is subscribed.

A StateFlow compares with equals when you set it and again in each collector. A busy collector sees only the latest value, so A, B, A while it is busy shows nothing. update { } may run its lambda many times.

shareIn and stateIn launch one coroutine in your scope. WhileSubscribed(5_000) survives a return within 5 s; after a stop the upstream restarts from the top, behind the stale value unless replayExpirationMillis = 0.

Reading .value is not a subscription, an upstream failure leaves subscribers waiting, and shareIn per call leaks a coroutine per call. Use Eagerly for values that are only read, retry above the share, and one shared flow per program.
The limit: every value here arrives through emit inside Kotlin. A library that calls you back on its own thread needs a bridge, which is the next lesson.

explain.prompt: A friend asks two things: why did the quick waiter lose announcements under DROP_LATEST when only the diary keeper was slow, and why does tryEmit on a default MutableSharedFlow() fail while the subscriber is idle? Answer both with the slate picture, in a few sentences.
explain.answer: A MutableSharedFlow keeps one slate of replay + extraBufferCapacity values, and every subscriber reads it at their own place. A line can be wiped only once the slowest subscriber has taken it, so the slowest subscriber decides when the slate is full, for everyone. Under DROP_LATEST a value that finds the slate full is never written down, so the quick waiter never sees it either. The default flow has no slate at all. A value can only pass from an emit that is suspended and waiting to a subscriber that takes it, hand to hand. tryEmit can't wait, so with any subscriber present it returns false, idle or not. With no subscriber it returns true, and the value goes nowhere.

deeper.html:
The internals, for a curious day. The field names here are private and may change in any release, so don't build on them.

Every collector of a shared flow gets a slot object from an array that starts at size 2 and doubles when full: 2 for one or two subscribers, 4 for three or four, 8 for five. A SharedFlow slot holds the index of the next value its collector will read, plus that collector's suspended continuation. The slate is a ring buffer, also allocated lazily and doubled when needed, and it holds the buffered values followed by the suspended emit calls as placeholder objects. Its start, head, is the smaller of the slowest collector's index and the start of the replay cache. When the slowest collector moves on, head moves, the old cells are cleared, and waiting emitters are resumed as their values move onto the slate. Every change happens under one lock, and the coroutines to resume are collected and resumed after the lock is released. The KDoc puts the cost of an emit at O(N) in the number of subscribers.

A StateFlow slot is one atomic field: free, waiting, pending, or a suspended continuation. An update marks every slot pending and copies nothing, which is why the KDoc calls StateFlow allocation-free. Updates that race each other use a sequence number that is odd while an update is being delivered. A second writer that arrives in the middle only bumps it, and the first writer loops round to deliver the newest value.

Two APIs in this area are experimental in 1.11.0 and need @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class). resetReplayCache() empties the replay cache for new subscribers, while existing ones keep what they had; on a MutableStateFlow it throws UnsupportedOperationException: MutableStateFlow.resetReplayCache is not supported. SharedFlow.asFlow(), new in 1.11.0, hides the hot type from callers.

The suspend overload stateIn(scope) has no started. It launches the upstream in scope, suspends until the first value, and returns a StateFlow holding it: in one run, a settings flow whose first value took 300 ms made stateIn return at t=300. That fits a setting loaded once at start-up. An empty upstream throws NoSuchElementException: Flow is empty. An upstream that fails before its first value rethrows to the caller and also cancels the scope you passed, so choose that scope knowing it goes down with a failed load.
